claims.text: Cash is the money a business holds and can spend now: the notes and coins in the till and the balance in its bank account.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business needs enough cash to pay wages, rent, supplier invoices and its other dated bills on the day each falls due; a business that cannot pay as the dates arrive risks losing suppliers, workers and, at worst, the business itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit and cash are not the same measure: profit is earned when a sale is made, but the cash may arrive weeks later when the customer buys on credit, so a profitable business can still run short of cash for a time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash-flow forecast is a table of the cash a business expects to receive and to pay out each month ahead, together with the cash balance it expects to hold at the end of each month.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A simple forecast is built month by month: the opening balance starts the month, net cash flow is the month's inflows less its outflows, and the closing balance is the opening balance plus net cash flow, carried forward as the next month's opening balance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A cash-flow forecast matters because it shows a coming shortage months in advance, while an overdraft can still be arranged or spending re-timed, and it sets out in figures the case a business makes to a lender.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A forecast rests on estimates: if actual inflows or outflows differ from what was expected, the actual balances move away from the forecast, so the figures should be re-read against each month's actual cash.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An amendment to a forecast changes a month's inflow or outflow and must be carried through: the month's net cash flow is recomputed, its closing balance changes, and every later month's opening balance moves with it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A missing figure in a forecast is completed from the figures around it: a missing closing balance is the opening balance plus net cash flow, a missing net cash flow is inflows less outflows, and a missing opening balance is the previous month's closing balance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A negative closing balance means the business expects to hold less cash than its payments require in that month; it names the size of the expected shortage and the month it lands in.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Interpreting a forecast means comparing the closing balances across months: a one-month dip points to a timing problem, while balances that fall month after month point to outflows running ahead of inflows structurally.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A surplus closing balance has meaning too: cash held beyond need could pay down borrowing, earn interest or be spent ahead of a busy season, provided the later months stay healthy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A bank overdraft is an agreement letting a business spend beyond its bank balance up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount used; it bridges a short gap, and a bank is likely to set and review the limit because the bank carries the repayment risk.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Delaying supplier payments holds cash in the business longer, but a supplier that is paid late can respond by withdrawing early-payment discounts or serving the business later when stock runs short, so the saving can cost more than it saves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Asking debtors to pay more quickly brings cash in sooner - through a deposit, cash-only terms or a small discount for early settlement - though a discount costs revenue and pressing too hard can strain customer relationships.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The fitting remedy depends on the shape of the forecast: a one-month trough in a healthy year suits an overdraft or a delayed payment, while balances that sink month after month call for changing the inflows and outflows themselves or raising longer-term finance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working capital is the finance held for a business's day-to-day operations: its current assets - stock, money owed by debtors and cash - less its current liabilities, the payments due within a year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business with too little working capital can struggle to pay wages and suppliers on time, whatever its long-term prospects; too much, and resources sit idle in slow stock or unneeded cash that could earn a return elsewhere.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working capital and a cash-flow forecast answer different questions: the forecast shows whether the cash inside working capital will cover the months ahead, while the working-capital figure shows the cushion held today.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Working capital is measured at a point in time, as a snapshot of resources against near-term bills; what matters alongside the total is its composition, because stock and slow debtors must still turn into cash before they can pay a bill.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
